documents.unit: Office of the Provost, Teaching Support and Innovation
documents.title: AI at UO: Statement of Purpose, Policy FAQ and course-policy guidance
documents.stance_why: The page sets no university stance: it says AI use is 'decided at your own or your unit's discretion', requires only a syllabus statement, and offers three stances (Not Allowed, Allowed With Limits, Allowed No Limits) for instructors to choose from, so the document delegates.
documents.summary: Provost-office hub with the AI Council statement of purpose, baseline instructor duties (a syllabus AI statement, revise assessments), a rule that grade penalties for suspected AI misuse need a conduct-office finding, three sample stances for instructors, and 2026-27 faculty programming.

units.why: The statement of purpose is the Provost-approved "north star" for AI in teaching; it sets purpose and principles ("adopt AI purposefully to enhance the human capacity for ethical, critical, and creative thinking"), so it is an institution-wide framework (P56), informs only.
units.anchor: adopt AI purposefully to enhance the human capacity for ethical, critical, and creative thinking
units.frag_start: True to our liberal arts core

units.why: "Have a syllabus policy statement on what AI use is allowed" is an imperative to instructors listed under baseline responsibilities, so it is a must for instructors that every syllabus carry an AI statement (P09), set before the course.
units.anchor: Have a syllabus policy statement on what AI use is allowed
units.policy: Instructors have a syllabus policy statement on what AI use is allowed

units.why: The same sentence says the allowed use is "decided at your own or your unit's discretion", so the university sets no stance and hands the decision to instructors or units (P04); the unit-level part is only partly captured by P04.
units.anchor: decided at your own or your unit's discretion
units.policy: What AI use is allowed is decided at the instructor's own or the unit's discretion
units.fit_note: Also lets the unit (department) decide, which P04 names only for instructors; P85 not chosen because the unit option is secondary to instructor choice.

units.why: The sentence ties the decision to "the course's learning objectives", so the rule on how to decide follows objectives (P83), not just who decides.
units.anchor: based on the course's learning objectives
units.policy: The decision on what AI use is allowed is based on the course's learning objectives

units.why: "Stay aware of how well AI can complete your assignments and exams and revise them as needed" tells instructors to redesign assessment because of AI, so it is P35 and binding on instructors before the course.
units.anchor: revise them as needed to protect assessment integrity
units.policy: Instructors stay aware of how well AI can complete their assignments and exams and revise them as needed to protect assessment integrity

units.why: The FAQ says "a grade penalty specifically for suspected AI misconduct requires a formal finding" from the conduct office, which is the procedure for handling suspected misuse (P81); it restricts instructors, so must-not impose a penalty without it.
units.anchor: a grade penalty specifically for suspected AI misconduct requires a formal finding
units.frag_start: But a grade penalty specifically for suspected
units.policy: A grade penalty specifically for suspected AI misconduct requires a formal finding from the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards first

units.why: "You can always grade against your criteria" lets instructors give lower marks to suspected AI work by ordinary grading without a misconduct penalty; no type says this, so it is UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: You can always grade against your criteria.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors may always grade suspected AI-generated work against their ordinary criteria, separate from any misconduct penalty.

units.why: "You can ask students to use AI through UO-approved systems" permits instructors to assign AI use within approved tools; requiring or building in AI use is P79 rather than P92 because the sentence is about assigning AI work.
units.anchor: You can ask students to use AI through UO-approved systems
units.frag_start: You can ask students to use AI
units.policy: Instructors may ask students to use AI through UO-approved systems, such as Copilot Chat with data protection or AI features built into existing course platforms

units.why: The examples name "Copilot Chat with data protection" and platform AI (ALEKS, Westlaw CoCounsel) as UO-approved systems, an institution-wide list rather than a single course tool, so P92.
units.anchor: Copilot Chat with data protection
units.frag_start: You can ask students to use AI
units.policy: UO-approved AI systems include Copilot Chat with data protection and AI features built into existing course platforms (e.g., ALEKS in Math, Westlaw CoCounsel in Law)

units.why: "you must consider the security, accessibility, and cost of these tools" binds instructors who choose third-party-account tools; it is about evaluating a tool before choosing it (P117), covering privacy, access and cost.
units.anchor: you must consider the security, accessibility, and cost of these tools
units.frag_start: If you're teaching with a tool
units.policy: Instructors teaching with a tool that requires a third-party account must consider its security, accessibility, and cost
units.fit_note: Also names accessibility and cost, which P117 does not.

units.why: "provide the possibility to opt out" requires an alternative for students who do not want a third-party AI account, an equity and consent rule (P51).
units.anchor: provide the possibility to opt out
units.frag_start: If you're teaching with a tool
units.policy: Instructors who require a tool with a third-party account provide the possibility to opt out

units.why: "Every UO syllabus should say something about GenAI" is a university-level should that all syllabi carry an AI statement (P09), communicated at course start.
units.anchor: Every UO syllabus should say something about GenAI.

units.why: The policy "names what students can learn from working with AI, or from working without it": a good policy follows from the specific learning objective, which is P83 (align AI decisions with learning objectives).
units.anchor: names what students can learn from working with AI, or from working without it
units.frag_start: A good AI policy is learning-centered
units.policy: A good AI policy names what students can learn from working with AI, or from working without it, in the specific course

units.why: "Say what's allowed on the syllabus and in assignment instructions" tells instructors to state expectations in both places, which fits P09.
units.anchor: Say what's allowed on the syllabus and in assignment instructions

units.why: "Students move between courses with very different AI policies" explains why transparency matters, noting that rules differ course to course; closest to P11 (a course's rule governs only that course).
units.anchor: Students move between courses with very different AI policies.
units.fit_note: States the fact of differing policies as the reason for transparency, not a rule that permissions do not carry over.

units.why: "be ready to explain your reasoning if asked" asks instructors to give students the reasons behind their rules, which is P66.
units.anchor: be ready to explain your reasoning if asked

units.why: The page groups sample policies into "Three Broad Stances", named categories of AI use that instructors choose among, so P05.
units.anchor: Sample policies on the GenAI Course Policies page are grouped by which of these

units.why: Tier "Not Allowed" is defined as "Students may not use AI tools to produce course materials or assignments, in whole or part", a named tier that bans AI, so P05 with prohibit unit_stance.
units.anchor: Students may not use AI tools to produce course materials or assignments
units.frag_start: Students may not use AI tools
units.fit_note: Defines the Not Allowed tier; the ban itself would otherwise be P19.

units.why: Tier "Allowed, With Limits" says some tasks or tools are permitted and others are not, or "require citation and documentation of use"; a named middle tier, so P05 with restrict.
units.anchor: others aren't, or require citation and documentation of use.

units.why: Tier "Allowed, No Limits" says "AI is open for use across the course, typically still with a citation expectation", the open tier, so P05 with permit.
units.anchor: AI is open for use across the course, typically still with a citation expectation.

units.why: "A syllabus statement isn't enough on its own" and students "need to see AI expectations at the assignment level" tell instructors to state AI expectations in assignments as well, a P09 rule.
units.anchor: students need to see AI expectations at the assignment level, not just the course level

units.why: "Our AI-aware assignment template can help you carry your policy into individual assignments" is the institution supplying a template for instructors, so P110.
units.anchor: Our AI-aware assignment template can help you carry your policy into individual assignments.

units.why: "Communicate your rationale, not just the rule" is advice to explain the reasons behind AI rules, which is P66.
units.anchor: Communicate your rationale, not just the rule.

units.why: The Council summary wants "UO grades reflect real learning" and to confirm "the integrity of our curriculum and grades"; the reason is honest evaluation of learning, so P95 rather than P41.
units.anchor: confirming that grades reflect real learning and by making sure the skills we teach
units.policy: The Council aims to confirm that grades reflect real learning and that the skills taught remain meaningful

units.why: The recommendations aim to "ensure faculty set clear course policies on AI use, receive feedback on their approaches" and have adaptation visible in evaluation; making faculty AI adaptation count in evaluation is not covered by any type, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: have their work to adapt courses made visible in evaluation
units.frag_start: UO teaching expectations are AI aware:
units.uncovered_note: Faculty work adapting courses to AI is to be made visible in faculty evaluation, with feedback on their course AI policies.

units.why: The Council wants "both embracing AI tools to prepare students for their careers and futures" and deepening human skills, giving a career reason to embrace AI (P44).
units.anchor: both embracing AI tools to prepare students for their careers and futures
units.frag_start: The prevalence of generative AI requires
units.policy: The university embraces AI tools to prepare students for their careers and futures

units.why: The aim to "teach the durable human skills a residential university is uniquely positioned to cultivate" repositions the curriculum around human skills in light of AI; this is neither a rule nor a standard rationale type, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: we teach the durable human skills a residential university is uniquely positioned to cultivate
units.uncovered_note: The university repositions its curriculum to teach durable human skills as AI changes education.

units.why: "endorsed by the AI Council August 19, 2026" states who adopted the recommendations and when, which is P84.
units.anchor: endorsed by the AI Council August 19, 2026
units.policy: The 18 GenAI in Teaching and Learning recommendations were endorsed by the AI Council on August 19, 2026

units.why: A goal that "we have a shared policy framework" says the institution will build an institution-wide framework, closest to P56.
units.anchor: we have a shared policy framework
units.frag_start: In fulfilling this full set of 18
units.policy: The university aims to have a shared policy framework for GenAI in teaching and learning

units.why: The Year of Action invites faculty to "Build your own AI literacy in conversation with expert colleagues", faculty support in learning AI (P63).
units.anchor: Build your own AI literacy

units.why: "Revise your own assignments in a community of practice with fellow instructors" and the stipended Communities of Practice are faculty support programs (P63).
units.anchor: Revise your own assignments

units.why: The Teaching Day of Exchange offers "strategies for both integrating AI and motivating meaningful student work without it", a faculty learning event (P63).
units.anchor: strategies for both integrating AI and motivating meaningful student work without it
units.frag_start: A full day of programming centered

units.why: "researching student views" and "Educational Research" communities indicate the university gathers evidence about how AI affects students and learning (P55).
units.anchor: researching student views
units.fit_note: Researches student views, not only learning outcomes.

documents.unit: Office of the Provost, Teaching Support and Innovation
documents.title: AI & Academic Integrity
documents.stance_why: The page sets no AI-use stance; it covers integrity procedure and says plagiarism 'may include artificial intelligence (AI) content generators', leaving what is allowed to instructors, so it delegates.
documents.summary: Short integrity page: the Student Conduct Code plagiarism definition now covers uncited AI content generators, UO does not support AI detectors, and suspected cases with grade penalties go through the conduct office.

units.why: "Creating a strong culture of academic integrity at UO is a collective, university-wide project" grounds the integrity rules in community culture, so P95 (fairness and honesty rationale).
units.anchor: Creating a strong culture of academic integrity at UO is a collective, university-wide project
units.frag_start: Creating a strong culture of academic integrity

units.why: UO "updated the Ducks Have Integrity module that all incoming students take to include AI", mandatory AI-related integrity training for students, so P70.
units.anchor: updated the "Ducks Have Integrity" module that all incoming students take to include AI
units.policy: UO updated the "Ducks Have Integrity" module that all incoming students take to include AI

units.why: The module also aims "to bolster students' confidence in asking instructors about appropriate use", encouraging students to ask instructors (P10).
units.anchor: bolster students' confidence in asking instructors about appropriate use
units.fit_note: Framed as a training goal that builds confidence to ask, not a direct instruction to ask.

units.why: The Student Conduct Code now says plagiarism "may include artificial intelligence (AI) content generators and generative AI tools" when use is not cited, classing uncited AI use as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: may include artificial intelligence (AI) content generators and generative AI tools
units.policy: Under the Student Conduct Code, plagiarism may include artificial intelligence (AI) content generators and generative AI tools when use is not cited

units.why: "UO does not currently support AI detection tools" is a statement that detectors are not supported, so P39 (do not rely on AI detectors).
units.anchor: UO does not currently support AI detection tools

units.why: The quoted note says detectors "may not be effective and can result in false positives", the reliability warning of P39.
units.anchor: may not be effective and can result in false positives
units.policy: Online AI detection tools like Turnitin.com or GPTZero may not be effective and can result in false positives

units.why: "we would not consider the percentages provided by these tools as dispositive on their own" sets a standard that detector scores are not sufficient evidence, P69.
units.anchor: we would not consider the percentages provided by these tools as dispositive on their own
units.policy: The conduct office does not consider detector percentages dispositive on their own

units.why: "instructors should not impose a grade penalty without a finding from that office" is a procedural rule for suspected misconduct (P81), should-not for instructors.
units.anchor: instructors should not impose a grade penalty without a finding from that office
units.frag_start: In other words, instructors should not
units.policy: Instructors should not impose a grade penalty without a finding from the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards

units.why: Instructors "should" use the Reporting Academic Misconduct Form "within five business days of discovery", a required form and deadline (P81).
units.anchor: submit information and documentation about the alleged incident within five business days of discovery
units.policy: Instructors use SCCS's Reporting Academic Misconduct Form to submit information and documentation about the alleged incident within five business days of discovery

units.why: "Contact SCCS with questions about academic integrity" directs instructors to an office for help, which is pointing to further resources (P115).
units.anchor: Contact SCCS with questions about academic integrity or other potential student conduct issues

documents.unit: Office of the Dean of Students
documents.title: Student Conduct Updates for Faculty (plagiarism definition and ChatGPT guidance)
documents.stance_why: The letter encourages 'all faculty to consider and determine your own course philosophy and expectations around the use of generative AI tools', so it hands the decision to instructors and sets no stance of its own.
documents.summary: 2023 Dean of Students letter on conduct code changes: AI content counts as plagiarism, grade-penalty cases go to the conduct office, and faculty are urged to set and discuss their own AI expectations. It also lists detection methods and cautions on detectors.

units.why: The Board-approved change "any academic misconduct concerns to be adjudicated by SCCS where a grade penalty may result", a formal reporting procedure (P81).
units.anchor: any academic misconduct concerns to be adjudicated by SCCS where a grade penalty may result
units.frag_start: The Board of Trustees approved a change
units.policy: Academic misconduct concerns where a grade penalty may result must be adjudicated by SCCS

units.why: The change was made "to ensure that the protections and rights embedded in the formal student conduct process are afforded to students"; fairness to accused students is nearest to P64, though it does not mention a right to respond.
units.anchor: protections and rights embedded in the formal student conduct process are afforded to students
units.frag_start: This change was implemented to ensure
units.policy: The change is implemented to ensure that the protections and rights of the formal student conduct process are afforded to students
units.fit_note: General procedural protections and rights, not specifically the right to respond to allegations; not AI-specific.

units.why: "You retain the ability to resolve academic misconduct concerns informally" lets instructors handle cases without a formal finding, which matches no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: You retain the ability to resolve academic misconduct concerns informally
units.frag_start: You retain the ability to resolve
units.uncovered_note: Instructors may still resolve academic misconduct concerns informally and are encouraged to consult SCCS about options.

units.why: Instructors are encouraged to use the reporting form "Even when not considering a grade penalty", a reporting procedure (P81) with should.
units.anchor: utilize the Reporting Academic Misconduct Form to submit incidents for our review
units.frag_start: Even when not considering a grade penalty

units.why: The formal process "allows us to have educational conversations with students about academic misconduct", an educative rather than only punitive response (P68).
units.anchor: have educational conversations with students about academic misconduct
units.frag_start: The formal student conduct process allows us
units.policy: The formal student conduct process allows educational conversations with students about academic misconduct, to find knowledge gaps and educate about expectations

units.why: "SCCS maintains records about any prior or future violations by a student" is a records practice for pattern detection that no type covers, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: SCCS maintains records about any prior or future violations by a student
units.uncovered_note: The conduct office keeps records of student violations so it can address patterns of behavior.

units.why: The updated Plagiarism definition says it "may include artificial intelligence (AI) content generators and generative AI tools such as ChatGPT", classifying submitting AI-generated material as plagiarism (P36).
units.anchor: This may include artificial intelligence (AI) content generators and generative AI tools such as ChatGPT
units.policy: Plagiarism includes the submission of material generated by others, which may include AI content generators and generative AI tools such as ChatGPT

units.why: The letter urges instructors to "incorporate these definitions into your course syllabus and in discussions with students", a syllabus statement rule (P09).
units.anchor: incorporate these definitions into your course syllabus and in discussions with students
units.policy: Instructors incorporate the plagiarism definitions into their course syllabus and in discussions with students
units.fit_note: Also asks for discussion with students (P66).

units.why: "Allegations of plagiarism involving the use of generative AI tools have constituted over half of all academic misconduct reports" is evidence about AI misuse volume (P55).
units.anchor: have constituted over half of all academic misconduct reports submitted
units.fit_note: Counts misconduct reports rather than learning outcomes.

units.why: The Dean joins the Provost "in encouraging all faculty to consider and determine your own course philosophy and expectations", leaving the AI rule to instructors (P04).
units.anchor: determine your own course philosophy and expectations around the use of generative AI tools
units.frag_start: I join with the Office of the Provost
units.policy: Faculty determine their own course philosophy and expectations around the use of generative AI tools for each course

units.why: Faculty should "communicate those expectations in your course syllabus", the syllabus statement rule (P09).
units.anchor: communicate those expectations in your course syllabus
units.frag_start: I join with the Office of the Provost
units.policy: Faculty communicate their generative AI expectations in the course syllabus

units.why: Faculty should "discuss them in the first week of the term", talking through the rules with students, P66.
units.anchor: discuss them in the first week of the term
units.frag_start: I join with the Office of the Provost
units.policy: Faculty discuss their generative AI expectations with students in the first week of the term

units.why: "Sample course syllabus language can be found at teaching.uoregon.edu/ai" points instructors to sample statements, P110.
units.anchor: Sample course syllabus language can be found at

units.why: Running the assignment prompt through a generative AI tool and comparing with student work is a "method that can be used to detect potential violations", a detection practice (P40).
units.anchor: Running your specific assignment prompt through a generative AI tool
units.fit_note: Compares against AI-generated responses to the prompt rather than using software or logs.

units.why: The letter says AI users "will typically submit work that contains similar inaccuracies" and lists fabricated content as a sign of AI use, an identification method (P40).
units.anchor: will typically submit work that contains similar inaccuracies
units.frag_start: A distinctive feature of AI generated content
units.fit_note: Signs of AI use in content; not software or logs.

units.why: "Comparing the assignment of concern with other work submitted by the student" for style changes is a process-evidence way to spot misuse, P40.
units.anchor: looking for distinct and significant changes in writing style
units.fit_note: Style comparison by the instructor, not a software check.

units.why: "Verifying quotes, sources, and citations used in the assignment" is another method to find fabricated AI references, P40.
units.anchor: Verifying quotes, sources, and citations used in the assignment.
units.fit_note: Manual verification of citations, not software.

units.why: "Writing your assignment prompts in a manner that makes generative AI use more obvious" changes assignment design in response to AI, P35.
units.anchor: Writing your assignment prompts in a manner that makes generative AI use more obvious

units.why: UO "has determined that the use of online AI detection tools like Turnitin.com or GPTZero may not be effective and can result in false positives", the unreliability claim of P39.
units.anchor: may not be effective and can result in false positives
units.frag_start: The University of Oregon has determined that
units.policy: UO has determined that online AI detection tools like Turnitin.com or GPTZero may not be effective and can result in false positives

units.why: "we would not consider the percentages provided by these tools as dispositive on their own" is an evidence standard for detector output (P69).
units.anchor: we would not consider the percentages provided by these tools as dispositive on their own
units.frag_start: If you choose to utilize these tools

units.why: "use these tools and the percentages generated by them as a starting point" permits detector use as a supporting factor, P40.
units.anchor: use these tools and the percentages generated by them as a starting point
units.frag_start: You may use these tools and
units.fit_note: Use as a starting point only, not as proof.

units.why: "without any additional information or an acknowledgement from the student ... there may not be enough to find that they engaged in a violation" sets what evidence is needed for a finding, P69.
units.anchor: there may not be enough to find that they engaged in a violation

units.why: "we encourage you to continue to refer these cases to SCCS for review when you have concerns" asks instructors to report suspected misconduct through the central office (P81).
units.anchor: we encourage you to continue to refer these cases to SCCS for review
units.frag_start: We can still have educational conversations

units.why: "We can still have educational conversations with students even when there is not enough information to find a violation" is an educative response to suspected misuse (P68).
units.anchor: We can still have educational conversations with students even when there is not enough
units.frag_start: We can still have educational conversations

units.why: Changes to the Code are proposed by a committee "comprised of students, staff, and faculty", describing how the policy was made (P84).
units.anchor: comprised of students, staff, and faculty appointed by ASUO, OA Council, and Faculty Senate
units.frag_start: The Board of Trustees considers changes
units.policy: The Board of Trustees considers changes to the Student Conduct Code proposed by the Student Conduct Advisory Committee, comprised of students, staff, and faculty
